questions.explanation: Assumption: An unstated idea on which the argument depends.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: According to the quick revision rules, what makes a strong argument?

options.A: It is relevant, significant, logical, and adequately supported
options.B: It is popular and emotionally appealing
options.C: It is long and complex
options.D: It attacks the opponent's character

questions.explanation: Strong argument: Relevant, significant, logical, and adequately supported.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: According to the quick revision rules, what must be checked in cause-and-effect questions?

options.A: Only the sequence of events
options.B: The causal connection; sequence or correlation alone is not proof
options.C: Only the popularity of the events
options.D: Only whether the events are emotionally appealing

questions.explanation: Cause and effect: Check causal connection; sequence or correlation alone is not proof.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is the recommended final exam approach for logical reasoning?

options.A: First identify the question type; then underline quantifiers and conditions; represent category relationships if needed; test each option strictly against the premises; and select only what is logically justified
options.B: First select the longest option; then check if it matches personal opinion
options.C: First ignore the instructions; then guess the answer
options.D: First use outside knowledge; then reject all premises that conflict with it

questions.explanation: First identify the question type; then underline quantifiers and conditions; represent category relationships if needed; test each option strictly against the premises; and select only what is logically justified. Practise timed questions after learning the rules.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a statement in the logical sense?

options.A: The examination begins at 10 a.m.
options.B: All applicants must carry an identity card.
options.C: Please close the door.
options.D: No bird is a mammal.

questions.explanation: Questions, commands, and requests are generally not statements because they do not assert a truth-valued proposition. 'Please close the door' is a request.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: The conditional 'If P, then Q' is false only when:

options.A: P is false and Q is true
options.B: P is true and Q is false
options.C: Both P and Q are false
options.D: Both P and Q are true

questions.explanation: The conditional is false only when P is true and Q is false.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: In 'Only graduates are eligible', which of the following is true?

options.A: All graduates are eligible
options.B: All eligible persons are graduates
options.C: Some graduates are not eligible
options.D: No graduate is eligible

questions.explanation: In 'only A are B', every B is A. 'Only graduates are eligible' means all eligible persons are graduates. It does not state that every graduate is eligible.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: 'P unless Q' is commonly understood as:

options.A: If Q, then P
options.B: If not Q, then P (and in many aptitude questions, P or Q)
options.C: If P, then not Q
options.D: P and Q are both false

questions.explanation: 'P unless Q' is commonly understood as 'if not Q, then P'. In many aptitude questions it can also be expressed as 'P or Q'.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: 'All students passed' and 'Some students did not pass' are an example of:

options.A: Contrary statements
options.B: Contradictory statements
options.C: Consistent statements
options.D: Equivalent statements

questions.explanation: They cannot both be true and cannot both be false when they refer to the same group and examination. This is a contradictory pair.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Contrary statements differ from contradictory statements in that contrary statements:

options.A: Cannot both be true but may both be false
options.B: Cannot both be false but may both be true
options.C: Are always equivalent
options.D: Are always consistent

questions.explanation: Contrary statements cannot both be true, but they may both be false. Contradictory statements cannot both be true or both be false.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: The negation test for a necessary assumption involves:

options.A: Temporarily denying the proposed assumption and checking whether the argument collapses
options.B: Checking whether the assumption is explicitly stated
options.C: Counting how many people believe the assumption
options.D: Replacing the assumption with its conclusion

questions.explanation: Use the negation test: temporarily deny the proposed assumption. If the argument collapses or loses its essential support, the assumption is likely necessary.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: An assumption in an argument:

options.A: Must be universally true in reality to be valid
options.B: Only needs to be a premise taken for granted within the particular argument and may be questionable in reality
options.C: Is always explicitly stated in the passage
options.D: Is the same as the conclusion

questions.explanation: An assumption does not have to be universally true. It only needs to be a premise taken for granted within the particular argument. It may be questionable in reality, but the question asks whether the argument relies on it.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an ad hominem argument?

options.A: The proposal is bad because it will increase costs
options.B: The proposal is bad because its supporter is dishonest
options.C: The proposal is bad because it violates the principle of fairness
options.D: The proposal is bad because it cannot be implemented with available resources

questions.explanation: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of addressing the claim or evidence. It is generally a weak form of reasoning.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a false dilemma?

options.A: Either we ban all cars or the environment will be destroyed
options.B: We should improve public transport because it reduces congestion
options.C: The policy is feasible because resources are available
options.D: The policy is fair because it treats all citizens equally

questions.explanation: A false dilemma presents only two choices when additional reasonable alternatives may exist. 'Either we ban all cars or the environment will be destroyed' ignores other alternatives.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a hasty generalisation?

options.A: All four students I met from that school are bright; therefore, all students in that school are bright
options.B: The policy is feasible because resources are available
options.C: The argument is strong because it directly addresses the issue
options.D: The measure is justified because it protects public health

questions.explanation: A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative examples.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a circular argument?

options.A: The book is reliable because it is trustworthy
options.B: The book is reliable because it was published by a reputable press
options.C: The book is reliable because experts reviewed it
options.D: The book is reliable because it cites primary sources

questions.explanation: A circular argument uses the conclusion itself, or a restatement of it, as support instead of providing independent evidence.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a slippery-slope argument?

options.A: If we allow students to use calculators, soon they will forget all basic arithmetic and education will collapse
options.B: If we allow calculators, students may complete calculations faster
options.C: Calculators are useful tools for complex calculations
options.D: Calculators should be permitted because they are widely available

questions.explanation: A slippery-slope argument claims that one step will inevitably lead to a chain of extreme consequences without adequately establishing the causal links.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which type of argument supports or opposes an action by explaining its likely benefits, harms, costs, or wider effects?

options.A: Argument from feasibility
options.B: Argument from consequences
options.C: Argument from principle
options.D: Ad hominem argument

questions.explanation: An argument from consequences supports or opposes an action by explaining its likely benefits, harms, costs, or wider effects.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: An argument that evaluates whether a proposal can practically be implemented, considering resources, time, infrastructure, authority, and operational constraints, is called:

options.A: Argument from consequences
options.B: Argument from principle
options.C: Argument from feasibility
options.D: Circular argument

questions.explanation: An argument from feasibility evaluates whether a proposal can practically be implemented, considering resources, time, infrastructure, authority, and operational constraints.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: An argument that refers to a rule, right, duty, fairness, equality, or other normative principle is called:

options.A: Argument from feasibility
options.B: Argument from consequences
options.C: Argument from principle
options.D: Hasty generalisation

questions.explanation: An argument from principle supports or opposes an action by referring to a rule, right, duty, fairness, equality, or other normative principle.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: In standard passage-based reasoning, which of the following is the best approach?

options.A: Use the passage as primary evidence and avoid outside facts unless explicitly required
options.B: Use outside knowledge as the primary evidence
options.C: Ignore the passage and rely on general knowledge
options.D: Use only personal experience

questions.explanation: In standard passage-based reasoning, use the passage as the primary evidence and avoid outside facts unless the question explicitly requires general knowledge.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about extreme words such as 'always', 'never', 'all', and 'only' in inference questions?

options.A: They always make the option correct
options.B: They are automatically wrong and should be rejected
options.C: They require evidence strong enough to justify an absolute claim; a passage describing a few cases usually cannot support such a conclusion
options.D: They have no effect on the validity of an inference

questions.explanation: These words make strong or absolute claims. A passage that describes a few cases usually cannot support an absolute conclusion. They are not automatically wrong, but they require strong evidence.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a confounding factor?

options.A: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents both increase in summer because hot weather increases both
options.B: Heavy rain causes rivers to rise
options.C: A flood damages houses and roads
options.D: A factory releases wastewater, causing fish deaths

questions.explanation: A confounding factor is a third variable (hot weather) that influences both variables being studied (ice cream sales and drowning incidents) and can create or distort an apparent relationship between them.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following illustrates reverse causation?

options.A: Assuming that watching violent TV causes aggression, when in fact aggressive children may prefer violent TV
options.B: Heavy rain causes flooding
options.C: A flood damages crops and roads
options.D: Poor soil and pests cause crop loss

questions.explanation: Reverse causation occurs when the assumed direction of cause and effect is reversed: the supposed effect may actually influence the supposed cause.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of positive feedback?

options.A: A change that amplifies itself, such as more ice melting leading to more heat absorption and further melting
options.B: A change that stabilises the system
options.C: A change that reduces the initial cause
options.D: A change that has no effect

questions.explanation: Positive feedback amplifies a change, while negative feedback tends to reduce or stabilise it.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following illustrates negative feedback?

options.A: A thermostat turning off the heater when the room reaches the desired temperature
options.B: More ice melting leading to more heat absorption
options.C: A flood damaging more houses
options.D: A factory releasing more wastewater, causing more fish deaths

questions.explanation: Negative feedback tends to reduce or stabilise a change. A thermostat turning off the heater stabilises the temperature.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is the contrapositive of 'If the application is complete, it will be processed'?

options.A: If the application is processed, it is complete
options.B: If the application is not processed, it is not complete
options.C: If the application is not complete, it will not be processed
options.D: If the application is processed, it is not complete

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of 'If P, then Q' is 'If not Q, then not P'. Here, 'If the application is not processed, then it is not complete'.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: The inverse of 'If P, then Q' is:

options.A: If Q, then P
options.B: If not P, then not Q
options.C: If not Q, then not P
options.D: If P, then not Q

questions.explanation: The inverse is 'If not P, then not Q'. It is not generally equivalent to the original, although it is equivalent to the converse.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: 'If P then Q; Q; therefore P' is an example of:

options.A: Valid modus ponens
options.B: Valid modus tollens
options.C: The fallacy of affirming the consequent
options.D: The fallacy of denying the antecedent

questions.explanation: This is the invalid form of affirming the consequent. Q may have occurred for another reason.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: 'If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q' is an example of:

options.A: Valid modus ponens
options.B: Valid modus tollens
options.C: The fallacy of affirming the consequent
options.D: The fallacy of denying the antecedent

questions.explanation: This is the invalid form of denying the antecedent. Q may still occur for another reason.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: 'If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P' is an example of:

options.A: Valid modus tollens (contrapositive reasoning)
options.B: Invalid affirming the consequent
options.C: Invalid denying the antecedent
options.D: A circular argument

questions.explanation: This is valid modus tollens, which follows the contrapositive. 'If P then Q' is equivalent to 'If not Q then not P'.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about a contradiction?

options.A: It occurs when a proposition and its negation are both asserted, or when a set of claims cannot all be true together
options.B: It occurs when two propositions are logically equivalent
options.C: It occurs when a proposition is true
options.D: It occurs when an argument is strong

questions.explanation: A contradiction occurs when a proposition and its negation are both asserted, or when a set of claims cannot all be true together.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Two propositions are logically equivalent when:

options.A: They have the same truth value under every possible assignment of truth values
options.B: They sometimes have the same truth value
options.C: They can never both be true
options.D: They are both false in every case

questions.explanation: Two propositions are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value under every possible assignment of truth values.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the converse, inverse, and contrapositive of 'If P, then Q'?

options.A: Converse: If Q then P; Inverse: If not P then not Q; Contrapositive: If not Q then not P
options.B: Converse: If not Q then not P; Inverse: If Q then P; Contrapositive: If not P then not Q
options.C: Converse: If not P then not Q; Inverse: If not Q then not P; Contrapositive: If Q then P
options.D: All three are logically equivalent to the original

questions.explanation: The converse is 'If Q then P'; the inverse is 'If not P then not Q'; the contrapositive is 'If not Q then not P'. Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between 'All A are B' and 'All B are A'?

options.A: They are logically equivalent
options.B: 'All A are B' does not imply 'All B are A'; the conversion is invalid
options.C: 'All B are A' implies 'All A are B'
options.D: Both statements are always false

questions.explanation: From 'All A are B', one can conclude that all A lie within B, but not that B lies entirely within A. The conversion is invalid.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which conversions are valid according to the notes?

options.A: 'No A is B' to 'No B is A' and 'Some A are B' to 'Some B are A'
options.B: 'All A are B' to 'All B are A' and 'Some A are not B' to 'Some B are not A'
options.C: 'All A are B' to 'All B are A' only
options.D: No conversions are valid in logic

questions.explanation: 'No A is B' can be converted to 'No B is A' because the groups are mutually exclusive. 'Some A are B' can be converted to 'Some B are A' because the same overlapping members belong to both groups.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Under what condition should an either-or conclusion be selected?

options.A: Whenever two conclusions appear different
options.B: When two alternatives are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive under the question's logical conditions
options.C: Whenever the conclusion sounds reasonable
options.D: Whenever the conclusion is popular

questions.explanation: An either-or conclusion is used when two alternatives are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive under the question's logical conditions. It should not be selected merely because two conclusions appear different.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which statement best describes a possibility conclusion?

options.A: It must be true in every arrangement
options.B: It can be true without contradicting the premises; possibility is weaker than certainty
options.C: It contradicts the premises
options.D: It is always false

questions.explanation: A possibility conclusion is one that can be true without contradicting the premises. Possibility is weaker than certainty: a possible conclusion need not be true in every arrangement.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: In syllogism questions, 'Some A are B' does NOT necessarily mean:

options.A: At least one A is also B
options.B: Some B are A
options.C: All A are B
options.D: There is an overlap between A and B

questions.explanation: 'Some A are B' means at least one A is also B. It does not mean 'all A are B', and it does not necessarily mean 'some A are not B'.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: An argument can be valid in structure even when:

options.A: One or more premises are factually false
options.B: The conclusion is true
options.C: All premises are true
options.D: The reasoning is invalid

questions.explanation: Truth concerns whether a statement matches reality. Validity concerns whether a conclusion follows logically from its premises. An argument can be valid in structure even when one or more premises are factually false.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes deduction from induction?

options.A: Deduction gives probable conclusions; induction gives guaranteed conclusions
options.B: Deduction gives conclusions that must follow if premises are true; induction gives probable conclusions that are not guaranteed
options.C: Both give guaranteed conclusions
options.D: Both give only probable conclusions

questions.explanation: Deduction aims at a conclusion that must follow if the premises are true and the reasoning is valid. Induction uses observations or examples to support a probable conclusion, but the conclusion is not guaranteed.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: In statement-based reasoning questions, what should a candidate do if a premise conflicts with everyday experience?

options.A: Reject the premise immediately
options.B: Treat the supplied information as the basis of the answer and not reject the premise merely because it conflicts with everyday experience
options.C: Replace the premise with personal knowledge
options.D: Ignore the question

questions.explanation: Treat the information supplied in the question as the basis of the answer. Do not reject a premise merely because it conflicts with everyday experience, and do not introduce outside information unless the question expressly asks for factual knowledge.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is a hidden assumption connecting evidence to a conclusion?

options.A: The reliability of the information used as evidence
options.B: The length of the argument
options.C: The popularity of the conclusion
options.D: The emotional tone of the argument

questions.explanation: A hidden assumption is an unstated belief connecting the evidence to the conclusion. It may concern the reliability of information, the relevance of evidence, or the expected effect of an action.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: When evaluating strong and weak arguments, which of the following should be ignored?

options.A: Whether the argument addresses the exact issue
options.B: Whether the premise is credible
options.C: Emotional language and unrelated details
options.D: Whether the conclusion follows

questions.explanation: Check whether each argument addresses the exact issue, whether its reason is significant, whether the premise is credible, and whether the conclusion follows. Ignore emotional language and unrelated details.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about statistics in arguments?

options.A: Any statistic makes an argument strong
options.B: Statistics must be relevant, reliable, correctly interpreted, and sufficiently connected to the conclusion
options.C: Statistics are always irrelevant
options.D: Statistics are only useful in mathematics

questions.explanation: Statistics must be relevant, reliable, correctly interpreted, and sufficiently connected to the conclusion. Using statistics alone does not make an argument strong.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following best describes a factual inference?

options.A: A conclusion supported by the facts or data supplied, not going beyond what those facts reasonably establish
options.B: A conclusion based on personal opinion
options.C: A conclusion that adds outside knowledge
options.D: A guess without evidence

questions.explanation: A factual inference is a conclusion supported by the facts or data supplied. It must not go beyond what those facts reasonably establish.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: An implied idea in a passage is:

options.A: Directly stated in the passage
options.B: Not directly stated but reasonably suggested by the wording, context, or relationship between the supplied facts
options.C: Unrelated to the passage
options.D: Contradicted by the passage

questions.explanation: An implied idea is not directly stated but is reasonably suggested by the wording, context, or relationship between the supplied facts.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the relationship between temporal order and causation?

options.A: Temporal order is necessary for many causal relationships but is not sufficient to prove causation
options.B: Temporal order always proves causation
options.C: Temporal order is irrelevant to causation
options.D: Causation always occurs without temporal order

questions.explanation: Temporal order is necessary for many causal relationships, but it is not sufficient to prove causation.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: In 'P if Q', which condition is sufficient and which is necessary?

options.A: Q is sufficient for P; P is necessary for Q
options.B: P is sufficient for Q; Q is necessary for P
options.C: Both P and Q are necessary
options.D: Neither P nor Q is sufficient

questions.explanation: In 'P if Q', Q is sufficient for P, written Q → P. In 'P only if Q', Q is necessary for P.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: In 'P only if Q', which condition is necessary and which is sufficient?

options.A: Q is necessary for P; Q does not alone guarantee P
options.B: P is necessary for Q; P guarantees Q
options.C: Both P and Q are sufficient
options.D: Neither P nor Q is necessary

questions.explanation: 'P only if Q' means Q is necessary for P. It does not mean that Q alone guarantees P.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following correctly represents 'P only if Q'?

options.A: Q → P
options.B: P → Q
options.C: P ↔ Q
options.D: ¬P → Q

questions.explanation: 'P only if Q' means Q is necessary for P and is written P → Q.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following correctly represents 'P if Q'?

options.A: P → Q
options.B: Q → P
options.C: P ↔ Q
options.D: ¬Q → P

questions.explanation: 'P if Q' means Q is sufficient for P and is written Q → P.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following correctly represents 'P if and only if Q'?

options.A: P → Q only
options.B: Q → P only
options.C: P → Q and Q → P
options.D: Neither P → Q nor Q → P

questions.explanation: 'P if and only if Q' means P and Q imply each other: P → Q and Q → P. Both are necessary and sufficient for one another.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is a particular statement?

options.A: All applicants must carry an identity card
options.B: Every student passed the examination
options.C: Some students passed the examination
options.D: Each member must pay the fee

questions.explanation: A particular statement makes a claim about at least one or some members of a group. 'Some students passed the examination' is a particular statement.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is a universal statement?

options.A: Some applicants were selected
options.B: A few students failed
options.C: Every candidate must submit the form
options.D: At least one member attended

questions.explanation: A universal statement makes a claim about every member of a group. 'Every candidate must submit the form' is a universal statement.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following statements is consistent?

options.A: All students passed and some students did not pass (same group and examination)
options.B: No bird is a mammal and all sparrows are birds
options.C: All A are B and no A is B
options.D: P is true and not P is true

questions.explanation: A set of statements is consistent if all of them can be true together without creating a logical contradiction. 'No bird is a mammal' and 'all sparrows are birds' can both be true.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following pairs of statements is contradictory?

options.A: 'All students passed' and 'Some students did not pass' (same group and examination)
options.B: 'All students passed' and 'All students failed'
options.C: 'Some students passed' and 'Some students failed'
options.D: 'No student passed' and 'No student failed'

questions.explanation: Two statements are contradictory when they cannot both be true and cannot both be false. 'All students passed' and 'Some students did not pass' are contradictory when they refer to the same group and examination.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is an indirect conclusion?

options.A: A conclusion that follows immediately from a single statement
options.B: A conclusion reached by combining two or more premises through a chain of valid reasoning
options.C: A conclusion that requires outside knowledge
options.D: A conclusion that contradicts the premises

questions.explanation: An indirect conclusion is reached by combining two or more premises through a chain of valid reasoning.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: In a syllogism, Venn diagrams are primarily used to:

options.A: Represent categories as circles and show inclusion, exclusion, and overlap to test whether a conclusion is certain, impossible, or only possible
options.B: Calculate numerical answers
options.C: Prove causation
options.D: Measure the strength of an argument

questions.explanation: Venn diagrams represent categories as circles. They help show inclusion, exclusion, and overlap between groups and make it easier to test whether a proposed conclusion is certain, impossible, or only possible.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: From 'All A are B', which of the following necessarily follows?

options.A: All B are A
options.B: Every A is inside B
options.C: Some A are not B
options.D: No A is B

questions.explanation: From 'All A are B', every A is inside B. It does not establish that every B is A, and it does not establish that any A exists unless existence is separately given.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: From 'No A is B', which of the following follows?

options.A: All A are B
options.B: If something is A, it cannot be B, and vice versa
options.C: Some A are B
options.D: All B are A

questions.explanation: From 'No A is B', A and B have no overlap. Therefore, if something is A, it cannot be B, and vice versa.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about an explicit assumption?

options.A: It is stated openly rather than left unstated
options.B: It is always hidden
options.C: It is the conclusion of the argument
options.D: It is a fact presented as established information

questions.explanation: Strictly speaking, an explicit assumption is stated openly rather than left unstated. In many aptitude questions, the task is to distinguish what is stated from what is implicitly taken for granted.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: A necessary assumption is one that:

options.A: Must be true for the argument or recommendation to work as intended
options.B: Is always explicitly stated
options.C: Is universally true in reality
options.D: Is the same as the conclusion

questions.explanation: A necessary assumption is an unstated condition that must be true for the argument or recommendation to work as intended.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following makes an argument weak?

options.A: It is relevant and supported by credible reasons
options.B: It is irrelevant, unsupported, vague, based on an incorrect assumption, emotionally manipulative, or insufficient to support the conclusion
options.C: It directly addresses the issue
options.D: It provides significant evidence

questions.explanation: A weak argument is irrelevant, unsupported, vague, based on an incorrect assumption, emotionally manipulative, or insufficient to support the conclusion.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following best describes a fact-based argument?

options.A: It relies on verifiable information, evidence, data, or established conditions rather than merely personal preference
options.B: It relies on personal judgment
options.C: It relies on emotional appeals
options.D: It attacks the person making the claim

questions.explanation: A fact-based argument relies on verifiable information, evidence, data, or established conditions rather than merely personal preference.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: An opinion-based argument:

options.A: Can still be relevant but by itself may provide weaker support than reliable evidence
options.B: Is always irrelevant
options.C: Is always stronger than a fact-based argument
options.D: Cannot be evaluated at all

questions.explanation: An opinion-based argument expresses a personal judgment or preference. An opinion can still be relevant, but by itself it may provide weaker support than reliable evidence.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following distinguishes a certain inference from a probable inference?

options.A: A certain inference must follow from the premises; a probable inference is supported by the evidence but could be false
options.B: A certain inference could be false; a probable inference must follow from the premises
options.C: Both are guaranteed to be true
options.D: Both are guaranteed to be false

questions.explanation: A certain inference must follow from the premises. A probable inference is supported by the evidence but could be false.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about correlation and causation?

options.A: Correlation means two variables vary together; it does not by itself prove that one causes the other
options.B: Correlation always proves causation
options.C: Causation never requires evidence
options.D: Correlation and causation are identical

questions.explanation: Correlation means two variables vary together. It does not by itself prove that one causes the other. A causal inference requires additional evidence about timing, mechanism, alternative explanations, and confounding factors.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between a necessary condition and an outcome?

options.A: If the necessary condition is absent, the outcome cannot occur under the stated conditions
options.B: If the necessary condition is present, the outcome must occur
options.C: The necessary condition guarantees the outcome
options.D: The necessary condition is unrelated to the outcome

questions.explanation: A necessary condition is something that must be present for an outcome to occur. If it is absent, the outcome cannot occur under the stated conditions.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes a sufficient condition?

options.A: It is enough to guarantee an outcome under the stated logical rules, although the outcome may also occur for other reasons
options.B: It must be present for the outcome to occur
options.C: It prevents the outcome from occurring
options.D: It is unrelated to the outcome

questions.explanation: A sufficient condition is enough to guarantee an outcome under the stated logical rules, although the outcome may also occur for other reasons.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about a remote cause?

options.A: It is an earlier or more distant factor that contributes to the effect through intervening conditions
options.B: It is the factor closest in time to the effect
options.C: It has an immediate causal connection with the effect
options.D: It is a third variable that distorts a relationship

questions.explanation: A remote cause is an earlier or more distant factor that contributes to the effect through intervening conditions.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about an indirect cause?

options.A: It influences an outcome through one or more intermediate factors
options.B: It has an immediate causal connection with the effect
options.C: It is the factor closest in time to the effect
options.D: It is a third variable that influences both variables

questions.explanation: An indirect cause influences an outcome through one or more intermediate factors.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about an immediate cause?

options.A: It is the factor closest in time or causal sequence to the observed effect
options.B: It is an earlier factor contributing through intervening conditions
options.C: It influences through multiple intermediate factors
options.D: It is a third variable that creates an apparent relationship

questions.explanation: An immediate cause is the factor closest in time or causal sequence to the observed effect.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is true about a direct cause?

options.A: It has an immediate causal connection with the effect, without a substantial chain of intermediate events
options.B: It influences an outcome through multiple intermediate factors
options.C: It is an earlier or more distant factor
options.D: It is a third variable that influences both variables

questions.explanation: A direct cause has an immediate causal connection with the effect, without a substantial chain of intermediate events.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following best describes an effect?

options.A: An outcome or consequence produced or influenced by one or more causes
options.B: A factor that brings about an outcome
options.C: An unstated idea taken for granted
options.D: A statement that is always false

questions.explanation: An effect is an outcome or consequence produced or influenced by one or more causes.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following best describes a cause?

options.A: A factor or event that brings about or contributes to an outcome
options.B: An outcome produced by one or more factors
options.C: A conclusion drawn from evidence
options.D: An assumption taken for granted

questions.explanation: A cause is a factor or event that brings about or contributes to an outcome.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following best describes a cause-and-effect relationship?

options.A: A relationship that exists when one event or condition produces, contributes to, or helps explain another event or condition
options.B: A relationship in which two events occur at the same time without any connection
options.C: A relationship in which two events are unrelated
options.D: A relationship based only on sequence in time

questions.explanation: A cause-and-effect relationship exists when one event or condition produces, contributes to, or helps explain another event or condition.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following best describes a truth table?

options.A: A table that lists all possible truth-value combinations of propositions and shows the truth value of a compound statement for each combination
options.B: A table of mathematical values
options.C: A table that lists only true statements
options.D: A table that lists assumptions

questions.explanation: A truth table lists all possible truth-value combinations of propositions and shows the truth value of a compound statement for each combination.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT logically equivalent to 'If P, then Q'?

options.A: If not Q, then not P
options.B: If Q, then P
options.C: The contrapositive of 'If P, then Q'
options.D: Not Q implies not P

questions.explanation: 'If Q, then P' is the converse, which is not generally equivalent to the original. The contrapositive 'If not Q, then not P' is equivalent.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is logically equivalent to 'If P, then Q'?

options.A: If Q, then P
options.B: If not P, then not Q
options.C: If not Q, then not P
options.D: P and not Q

questions.explanation: The contrapositive 'If not Q, then not P' is logically equivalent to the original conditional.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the safest method when two options appear correct?

options.A: Select the longer option
options.B: Compare each option with the exact wording of the premises and prefer the option that is fully supported and introduces the fewest unstated assumptions
options.C: Select the option that sounds more reasonable in everyday life
options.D: Select the first option

questions.explanation: Compare each option with the exact wording of the premises. Prefer the option that is fully supported and introduces the fewest unstated assumptions.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Which of the following is the best first step in a statement-based question?

options.A: Read the instruction and identify whether the task asks for what definitely follows, what is assumed, which argument is strong, what can be inferred, or which event causes another
options.B: Select the longest option
options.C: Guess the answer based on personal experience
options.D: Skip the instructions and read only the options

questions.explanation: Read the instruction and identify whether the task asks for what definitely follows, what is assumed, which argument is strong, what can be inferred, or which event causes another.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Should a candidate use personal opinions in logical reasoning questions?

options.A: Yes, personal opinion is the basis of logical validity
options.B: No, apply the rules of reasoning and the information given; personal agreement or disagreement is not the test of logical validity
options.C: Yes, if the opinion is widely shared
options.D: No, but only for inference questions

questions.explanation: No. Apply the rules of reasoning and the information given. Personal agreement or disagreement is not the test of logical validity.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is logical reasoning?

options.A: The process of memorising facts for examinations
options.B: The systematic process of examining information, identifying relationships, evaluating evidence, and reaching conclusions that follow from given premises
options.C: The process of guessing answers based on personal experience
options.D: The process of applying mathematical formulas to solve problems

questions.explanation: Logical reasoning is the systematic process of examining information, identifying relationships, evaluating evidence, and reaching conclusions that follow from the given premises.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a premise in a reasoning question?

options.A: The final answer to a question
options.B: A statement or piece of information accepted as the starting point for a logical argument
options.C: A personal opinion about the topic
options.D: A question asked within the argument

questions.explanation: A premise is a statement or piece of information accepted as the starting point for a logical argument.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is the difference between validity and truth?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: Truth concerns whether a statement matches reality, while validity concerns whether a conclusion follows logically from its premises
options.C: Validity concerns reality, while truth concerns logical structure
options.D: Truth is about conclusions, while validity is about premises only

questions.explanation: Truth concerns whether a statement matches reality. Validity concerns whether a conclusion follows logically from its premises. An argument can be valid in structure even when one or more premises are factually false.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is the most important rule for statement-based reasoning questions?

options.A: Use personal knowledge to fill gaps in the question
options.B: Reject any premise that contradicts everyday experience
options.C: Treat the information supplied in the question as the basis of the answer
options.D: Always choose the most reasonable-sounding option

questions.explanation: Treat the information supplied in the question as the basis of the answer. Do not reject a premise merely because it conflicts with everyday experience, and do not introduce outside information unless the question expressly asks for factual knowledge.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is the difference between deduction and induction?

options.A: Deduction uses examples, while induction uses rules
options.B: Deduction aims at a conclusion that must follow if premises are true, while induction supports a probable conclusion from observations
options.C: Deduction is always false, while induction is always true
options.D: They are identical forms of reasoning

questions.explanation: Deduction aims at a conclusion that must follow if the premises are true and the reasoning is valid. Induction uses observations or examples to support a probable conclusion, but the conclusion is not guaranteed.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is the difference between an assumption and an inference?

options.A: They are the same concept
options.B: An assumption is an unstated idea taken for granted, while an inference is a conclusion drawn from provided information
options.C: An inference is unstated, while an assumption is explicitly stated
options.D: An assumption is always false, while an inference is always true

questions.explanation: An assumption is an unstated idea that a speaker or argument takes for granted. An inference is a conclusion drawn from the information provided. An assumption supports the argument; an inference is derived from it.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a statement in logical reasoning?

options.A: A question that can be answered
options.B: A command or request
options.C: A declarative sentence that asserts something and can be evaluated as true or false
options.D: A personal opinion that cannot be tested

questions.explanation: A statement is a declarative sentence that asserts something and can be evaluated as true or false. Questions, commands, and requests are generally not statements because they do not assert a truth-valued proposition.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a simple statement?

options.A: A statement that combines multiple propositions using AND or OR
options.B: A statement that expresses one proposition without joining it to another proposition through a logical connector
options.C: A statement that is always true
options.D: A statement that contains only one word

questions.explanation: A simple statement expresses one proposition without joining it to another proposition through a logical connector. Example: 'The examination begins at 10 a.m.'

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a compound statement?

options.A: A statement that contains only one proposition
options.B: A question with multiple answers
options.C: A statement formed by combining two or more propositions using logical connectors such as AND, OR, NOT, IF-THEN, or IF AND ONLY IF
options.D: A statement that is impossible to evaluate

questions.explanation: A compound statement is formed by combining two or more propositions using logical connectors such as AND, OR, NOT, IF-THEN, or IF AND ONLY IF.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does the conjunction 'P and Q' mean in logic?

options.A: It is true when at least one of P or Q is true
options.B: It is true only when both P and Q are true
options.C: It is true only when P is true and Q is false
options.D: It is always false

questions.explanation: The conjunction 'P and Q' is true only when both P and Q are true. If either part is false, the conjunction is false.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does 'or' mean in standard logical reasoning?

options.A: It always means exclusive or (one or the other, not both)
options.B: It is true only when exactly one of P or Q is true
options.C: Unless indicated otherwise, logical OR is inclusive: 'P or Q' is true when at least one is true, including when both are true
options.D: It means neither P nor Q is true

questions.explanation: Unless the question indicates an exclusive meaning, logical OR is inclusive: 'P or Q' is true when at least one of P or Q is true, including when both are true.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does 'not' mean in logic?

options.A: It affirms the proposition
options.B: It reverses the truth value of a proposition
options.C: It makes a proposition neither true nor false
options.D: It combines two propositions

questions.explanation: Negation reverses the truth value of a proposition. If P is true, NOT P is false; if P is false, NOT P is true.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does 'if P, then Q' mean?

options.A: Q is sufficient for P
options.B: P is the necessary condition and Q is the sufficient condition
options.C: Whenever P occurs, Q must follow; P is the sufficient condition and Q is the necessary condition
options.D: P and Q are unrelated

questions.explanation: It means that whenever P occurs, Q must follow. P is the sufficient condition and Q is the necessary condition. The conditional is false only when P is true and Q is false.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does 'P only if Q' mean?

options.A: Q is necessary for P; it is written as P → Q, and it does not mean Q alone guarantees P
options.B: P is necessary for Q
options.C: Q guarantees P
options.D: P and Q are equivalent

questions.explanation: 'P only if Q' means that Q is necessary for P. It is written as P → Q. It does not mean that Q alone guarantees P.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does 'P if Q' mean?

options.A: P is necessary for Q
options.B: Q is sufficient for P; it is written as Q → P
options.C: Q is necessary for P
options.D: P and Q are contradictory

questions.explanation: 'P if Q' means that Q is sufficient for P. It is written as Q → P.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does 'P if and only if Q' mean?

options.A: P implies Q but Q does not imply P
options.B: Q implies P but P does not imply Q
options.C: P and Q imply each other: both are necessary and sufficient for one another
options.D: P and Q can never both be true

questions.explanation: 'P if and only if Q' means P and Q imply each other: P → Q and Q → P. Both are necessary and sufficient for one another.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a universal statement?

options.A: A statement about some members of a group
options.B: A claim about every member of a group, using words like 'all', 'every', or 'each'
options.C: A statement that is always false
options.D: A question about a group

questions.explanation: A universal statement makes a claim about every member of a group. Common words are 'all', 'every', and 'each'. Example: 'All applicants must carry an identity card.'

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a particular statement?

options.A: A statement about every member of a group
options.B: A claim about at least one or some members of a group, using words like 'some', 'a few', or 'at least one'
options.C: A statement that cannot be tested
options.D: A command given to a group

questions.explanation: A particular statement makes a claim about at least one or some members of a group. Common words are 'some', 'a few', and 'at least one'.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does 'None A are B' mean in categorical statements?

options.A: Some A are B
options.B: All A are B
options.C: No member of group A belongs to group B; the two groups have no members in common
options.D: Some B are not A

questions.explanation: 'None A are B' means that no member of group A belongs to group B. The two groups have no members in common.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does 'Some A are B' mean in syllogism questions?

options.A: All A are B
options.B: At least one A is also B; it does not mean all A are B, and it does not necessarily mean some A are not B
options.C: No A is B
options.D: Some A are not B

questions.explanation: 'Some A are B' means at least one A is also B. It does not mean 'all A are B', and it does not necessarily mean 'some A are not B'.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What does 'Some A are not B' mean?

options.A: No A is B
options.B: All A are outside B
options.C: At least one member of A is outside group B; it does not mean every member of A is outside B
options.D: All B are A

questions.explanation: 'Some A are not B' means at least one member of A is outside group B. It does not mean that every member of A is outside B.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: How should the word 'only' be interpreted in 'Only A are B'?

options.A: Every A is B
options.B: Every B is A; it does not state that every A is B
options.C: Some A are B
options.D: No A is B

questions.explanation: In 'Only A are B', every B is A; it does not state that every A is B. For example, 'Only graduates are eligible' means all eligible persons are graduates.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: How should 'unless' be interpreted?

options.A: It always means 'if and only if'
options.B: 'P unless Q' is commonly understood as 'if not Q, then P'; in many aptitude questions it can also be expressed as 'P or Q'
options.C: It means 'P and Q are unrelated'
options.D: It means 'P implies Q'

questions.explanation: 'P unless Q' is commonly understood as 'if not Q, then P'. In many aptitude questions it can also be expressed as 'P or Q'. Read the exact wording and context carefully.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a contradictory pair of statements?

options.A: Two statements that cannot both be true but may both be false
options.B: Two statements that cannot both be true and cannot both be false
options.C: Two statements that are always both true
options.D: Two statements that are unrelated

questions.explanation: Two statements are contradictory when they cannot both be true and cannot both be false. For example, 'All students passed' and 'Some students did not pass' are contradictory when they refer to the same group and examination.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is the difference between contrary and contradictory statements?

options.A: They are the same
options.B: Contrary statements cannot both be true but may both be false; contradictory statements cannot both be true or both be false
options.C: Contradictory statements may both be false; contrary statements cannot both be false
options.D: Contrary statements are always true together

questions.explanation: Contrary statements cannot both be true, but they may both be false. Contradictory statements cannot both be true or both be false.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a consistent set of statements?

options.A: A set of statements that are all false
options.B: A set of statements that are all true
options.C: A set of statements that can all be true together without creating a logical contradiction
options.D: A set of statements that contradict each other

questions.explanation: A set of statements is consistent if all of them can be true together without creating a logical contradiction.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: How should a candidate identify the main claim in a long statement?

options.A: By memorising the entire sentence
options.B: By identifying the subject, the claim made about it, limiting words such as all/some/only, and any condition or exception
options.C: By counting the number of words
options.D: By ignoring all quantifiers

questions.explanation: Identify the subject, the claim made about it, limiting words such as all/some/only, and any condition or exception. Separate supporting details from the central proposition.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a conclusion in logical reasoning?

options.A: A question asked about the premises
options.B: A proposition that is claimed to follow from one or more given statements or premises
options.C: An unstated idea taken for granted
options.D: A personal opinion

questions.explanation: A conclusion is a proposition that is claimed to follow from one or more given statements or premises.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: When does a conclusion logically follow from premises?

options.A: When it is merely possible given the premises
options.B: When it is likely to be true
options.C: When it must be true if the given premises are true
options.D: When it is consistent with the premises

questions.explanation: A conclusion follows when it must be true if the given premises are true. A conclusion that is merely possible, likely, or consistent with the premises does not necessarily follow.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a direct conclusion?

options.A: A conclusion reached by a long chain of reasoning
options.B: A conclusion that follows immediately from a single statement or a straightforward combination of given statements, without requiring unsupported assumptions
options.C: A conclusion that is always false
options.D: A conclusion based on personal opinion

questions.explanation: A direct conclusion follows immediately from a single statement or a straightforward combination of the given statements, without requiring unsupported assumptions.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an indirect conclusion?

options.A: A conclusion that follows immediately from one statement
options.B: A conclusion reached by combining two or more premises through a chain of valid reasoning
options.C: A conclusion that cannot be derived
options.D: A conclusion that is always uncertain

questions.explanation: An indirect conclusion is reached by combining two or more premises through a chain of valid reasoning.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a syllogism?

options.A: A form of inductive reasoning from examples
options.B: A form of deductive reasoning in which a conclusion is tested against two or more premises, commonly using categorical statements such as all, some, and no
options.C: A type of mathematical equation
options.D: A personal belief system

questions.explanation: A syllogism is a form of deductive reasoning in which a conclusion is tested against two or more premises, commonly using categorical statements such as all, some, and no.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: How can Venn diagrams help solve syllogisms?

options.A: They replace the need for premises
options.B: They represent categories as circles and help show inclusion, exclusion, and overlap between groups to test whether a conclusion is certain, impossible, or only possible
options.C: They prove conclusions by counting elements
options.D: They are used only for mathematical problems

questions.explanation: Venn diagrams represent categories as circles. They help show inclusion, exclusion, and overlap between groups and make it easier to test whether a proposed conclusion is certain, impossible, or only possible.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What follows from 'All A are B'?

options.A: Every B is A
options.B: Every A is inside B; it does not establish that every B is A, and it does not establish that any A exists unless existence is separately given
options.C: No A is B
options.D: Some A are not B

questions.explanation: Every A is inside B. It does not establish that every B is A, and it does not establish that any A exists unless existence is separately given or the examination convention explicitly assumes it.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What follows from 'No A is B'?

options.A: All A are B
options.B: Some A are B
options.C: A and B have no overlap; therefore, if something is A, it cannot be B, and vice versa
options.D: Some B are not A

questions.explanation: A and B have no overlap. Therefore, if something is A, it cannot be B, and vice versa.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What follows from 'Some A are B'?

options.A: All A are B
options.B: At least one item belongs to both A and B; it does not establish that all A are B or that all B are A
options.C: No A is B
options.D: All B are A

questions.explanation: At least one item belongs to both A and B. It does not establish that all A are B or that all B are A.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Can 'All A are B' be converted into 'All B are A'?

options.A: Yes, always
options.B: No, this is an invalid conversion; from 'All A are B' one can conclude that all A lie within B, but not that B lies entirely within A
options.C: Yes, if A and B are the same size
options.D: Only when some A are B

questions.explanation: No. This is an invalid conversion. From 'All A are B', one can conclude that all A lie within B, but not that B lies entirely within A.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Can 'No A is B' be converted into 'No B is A'?

options.A: No, never
options.B: Yes, this is a valid conversion because the two groups are mutually exclusive
options.C: Only if some A are B
options.D: Only if all A are B

questions.explanation: Yes. This is a valid conversion because the two groups are mutually exclusive.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Can 'Some A are B' be converted into 'Some B are A'?

options.A: No, never
options.B: Yes, the same overlapping members belong to both groups
options.C: Only when all A are B
options.D: Only when no A is B

questions.explanation: Yes. The same overlapping members belong to both groups.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an either-or conclusion?

options.A: A conclusion that is always true
options.B: A conclusion used when two alternatives are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive under the question's logical conditions
options.C: A conclusion that is always false
options.D: A conclusion that combines two unrelated statements

questions.explanation: An either-or conclusion is used when two alternatives are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive under the question's logical conditions. It should not be selected merely because two conclusions appear different.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a possibility conclusion?

options.A: A conclusion that must be true in every arrangement
options.B: A conclusion that can be true without contradicting the premises; possibility is weaker than certainty
options.C: A conclusion that is always false
options.D: A conclusion that is unrelated to the premises

questions.explanation: A possibility conclusion is one that can be true without contradicting the premises. Possibility is weaker than certainty: a possible conclusion need not be true in every arrangement.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is the common mistake in conclusion questions?

options.A: Testing whether the conclusion must be true
options.B: Treating a conclusion that sounds reasonable or is generally true as one that logically follows
options.C: Using Venn diagrams
options.D: Reading the premises carefully

questions.explanation: The common mistake is treating a conclusion that sounds reasonable or is generally true as one that logically follows. The test is necessity, not plausibility.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an assumption?

options.A: A stated fact in the argument
options.B: An unstated proposition that is taken for granted and on which a statement, proposal, or argument depends
options.C: The final conclusion of an argument
options.D: A question asked about the argument

questions.explanation: An assumption is an unstated proposition that is taken for granted and on which a statement, proposal, or argument depends.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an implicit assumption?

options.A: An assumption that is directly written in the statement
options.B: An assumption that is not directly written but is required or presupposed for the statement or argument to make sense
options.C: An assumption that is always false
options.D: An assumption that is unrelated to the argument

questions.explanation: An implicit assumption is not directly written in the statement but is required or presupposed for the statement or argument to make sense.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an explicit assumption?

options.A: An assumption that is hidden
options.B: Strictly speaking, an assumption stated openly rather than left unstated
options.C: An assumption that cannot be tested
options.D: An assumption that is always true

questions.explanation: Strictly speaking, an explicit assumption is stated openly rather than left unstated. In many aptitude questions, the task is to distinguish what is stated from what is implicitly taken for granted.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a necessary assumption?

options.A: An assumption that is always true in reality
options.B: An unstated condition that must be true for the argument or recommendation to work as intended
options.C: An assumption that is stated explicitly
options.D: An assumption that weakens the argument

questions.explanation: A necessary assumption is an unstated condition that must be true for the argument or recommendation to work as intended.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a hidden assumption?

options.A: An assumption that is clearly stated
options.B: An unstated belief connecting the evidence to the conclusion, possibly concerning reliability of information, relevance of evidence, or expected effect of an action
options.C: An assumption that is always false
options.D: A conclusion drawn from the premises

questions.explanation: A hidden assumption is an unstated belief connecting the evidence to the conclusion. It may concern the reliability of information, the relevance of evidence, or the expected effect of an action.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: How can a necessary assumption be tested?

options.A: By checking if it is popular
options.B: Using the negation test: temporarily deny the proposed assumption; if the argument collapses or loses essential support, the assumption is likely necessary
options.C: By checking if it is explicitly stated
options.D: By counting the number of words

questions.explanation: Use the negation test: temporarily deny the proposed assumption. If the argument collapses or loses its essential support, the assumption is likely necessary. If the argument remains intact, it may not be necessary.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What might an advertisement assume?

options.A: That every possible marketing belief is true
options.B: That the target audience wants the advertised benefit, can access the product, and considers the claimed feature relevant
options.C: That the product is always the cheapest
options.D: That competitors will fail

questions.explanation: An advertisement may assume that the target audience wants the advertised benefit, can access the product, and considers the claimed feature relevant. Select only assumptions supported by the wording, not every possible marketing belief.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What might a policy proposal assume?

options.A: That the problem does not exist
options.B: That the identified problem exists, the proposed measure can influence it, the responsible authority can implement it, and the expected benefits justify the costs
options.C: That costs are irrelevant
options.D: That no authority is needed

questions.explanation: A policy proposal may assume that the identified problem exists, the proposed measure can influence it, the responsible authority can implement the measure, and the expected benefits justify the costs.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Does an assumption have to be universally true?

options.A: Yes, always
options.B: No; it only needs to be a premise taken for granted within the particular argument, and it may be questionable in reality
options.C: Only if it is stated explicitly
options.D: Only in syllogisms

questions.explanation: No. It only needs to be a premise taken for granted within the particular argument. It may be questionable in reality, but the question asks whether the argument relies on it.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is the difference between an assumption and a fact?

options.A: They are the same
options.B: A fact is presented as established information, while an assumption is accepted without being directly established in the argument
options.C: An assumption is always true, while a fact may be false
options.D: A fact is unstated, while an assumption is stated

questions.explanation: A fact is presented as established information. An assumption is accepted without being directly established in the argument.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is the difference between an assumption and a conclusion?

options.A: They are identical
options.B: An assumption is an unstated supporting idea on which reasoning depends, while a conclusion is the claim that the reasoning attempts to establish
options.C: A conclusion supports the assumption
options.D: An assumption is always stated, while a conclusion is unstated

questions.explanation: An assumption is an unstated supporting idea on which the reasoning depends. A conclusion is the claim that the reasoning attempts to establish.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an argument in logical reasoning?

options.A: A heated disagreement between two people
options.B: A set of statements in which one or more premises are offered as support for a conclusion
options.C: A single statement that is always true
options.D: A question requiring an answer

questions.explanation: An argument is a set of statements in which one or more premises are offered as support for a conclusion.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a strong argument?

options.A: An argument that uses emotional language
options.B: An argument that is relevant to the issue, logically connected to the conclusion, and supported by credible or significant reasons
options.C: An argument supported by many people
options.D: An argument that is very long

questions.explanation: A strong argument is relevant to the issue, logically connected to the conclusion, and supported by credible or significant reasons. It directly addresses the question being asked.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a weak argument?

options.A: An argument that directly addresses the issue
options.B: An argument that is irrelevant, unsupported, vague, based on an incorrect assumption, emotionally manipulative, or insufficient to support the conclusion
options.C: An argument based on verifiable data
options.D: An argument that provides a significant reason

questions.explanation: A weak argument is irrelevant, unsupported, vague, based on an incorrect assumption, emotionally manipulative, or insufficient to support the conclusion.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What makes an argument relevant?

options.A: It uses difficult words
options.B: It directly concerns the issue under discussion and provides a reason for or against the proposed action or claim
options.C: It is supported by many people
options.D: It is emotionally appealing

questions.explanation: An argument is relevant when it directly concerns the issue under discussion and provides a reason for or against the proposed action or claim.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What makes an argument logical?

options.A: It uses statistics
options.B: It uses coherent reasoning, avoids contradictions, and provides premises that genuinely support its conclusion
options.C: It is popular
options.D: It is based on personal preference

questions.explanation: A logical argument uses coherent reasoning, avoids contradictions, and provides premises that genuinely support its conclusion.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a fact-based argument?

options.A: An argument based on personal preference
options.B: An argument that relies on verifiable information, evidence, data, or established conditions rather than merely personal preference
options.C: An argument that attacks the person making a claim
options.D: An argument that presents only two choices

questions.explanation: A fact-based argument relies on verifiable information, evidence, data, or established conditions rather than merely personal preference.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an opinion-based argument?

options.A: An argument based on verifiable data
options.B: An argument that expresses a personal judgment or preference; it can be relevant but may provide weaker support than reliable evidence
options.C: An argument that is always strong
options.D: An argument based on established conditions

questions.explanation: An opinion-based argument expresses a personal judgment or preference. An opinion can still be relevant, but by itself it may provide weaker support than reliable evidence.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an argument from consequences?

options.A: An argument based on rules and duties
options.B: An argument that supports or opposes an action by explaining its likely benefits, harms, costs, or wider effects
options.C: An argument that attacks the person
options.D: An argument based on popularity

questions.explanation: An argument from consequences supports or opposes an action by explaining its likely benefits, harms, costs, or wider effects.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an argument from feasibility?

options.A: An argument based on moral principles
options.B: An argument that evaluates whether a proposal can practically be implemented, considering resources, time, infrastructure, authority, and operational constraints
options.C: An argument based on emotions
options.D: An argument that presents only two choices

questions.explanation: An argument from feasibility evaluates whether a proposal can practically be implemented, considering resources, time, infrastructure, authority, and operational constraints.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an argument from principle?

options.A: An argument based on practical constraints
options.B: An argument that supports or opposes an action by referring to a rule, right, duty, fairness, equality, or other normative principle
options.C: An argument based on statistical data
options.D: An argument that attacks a person

questions.explanation: An argument from principle supports or opposes an action by referring to a rule, right, duty, fairness, equality, or other normative principle.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: How should strong and weak arguments be evaluated?

options.A: By checking emotional language
options.B: By checking whether each argument addresses the exact issue, whether its reason is significant, whether the premise is credible, and whether the conclusion follows
options.C: By counting how many people support it
options.D: By checking the length of the argument

questions.explanation: Check whether each argument addresses the exact issue, whether its reason is significant, whether the premise is credible, and whether the conclusion follows. Ignore emotional language and unrelated details.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Is an argument strong merely because many people support it?

options.A: Yes, popularity proves correctness
options.B: No; popularity does not prove correctness, and the argument must still be relevant and logically supported
options.C: Yes, if the majority is large enough
options.D: Only in democratic contexts

questions.explanation: No. Popularity does not prove correctness. The argument must still be relevant and logically supported.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: Is an argument strong merely because it uses statistics?

options.A: Yes, statistics always prove a point
options.B: No; statistics must be relevant, reliable, correctly interpreted, and sufficiently connected to the conclusion
options.C: Yes, if the numbers are large
options.D: Only if the statistics are recent

questions.explanation: No. Statistics must be relevant, reliable, correctly interpreted, and sufficiently connected to the conclusion.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is an ad hominem argument?

options.A: An argument that attacks the person making a claim instead of addressing the claim or evidence
options.B: An argument based on statistics
options.C: An argument from consequences
options.D: An argument from principle

questions.explanation: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of addressing the claim or evidence. It is generally a weak form of reasoning.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a false dilemma?

options.A: An argument that presents only two choices when additional reasonable alternatives may exist
options.B: An argument that attacks a person
options.C: An argument based on too few examples
options.D: An argument that uses the conclusion as support

questions.explanation: A false dilemma presents only two choices when additional reasonable alternatives may exist.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a hasty generalisation?

options.A: An argument that draws a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative examples
options.B: An argument that presents only two choices
options.C: An argument that attacks a person
options.D: An argument that uses the conclusion as support

questions.explanation: A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative examples.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a circular argument?

options.A: An argument that uses the conclusion itself, or a restatement of it, as support instead of providing independent evidence
options.B: An argument that presents only two choices
options.C: An argument based on too few examples
options.D: An argument that attacks a person

questions.explanation: A circular argument uses the conclusion itself, or a restatement of it, as support instead of providing independent evidence.

questions.subject: Mental Ability
questions.question: What is a slippery-slope argument?
